To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the cycling of matter from the interstellar medium (ISM) to stars, back to the ISM, and then back to the stars is the fundamental process that drives galaxy evolution, that the key to understanding this process lies in understanding the physics that governs how gas cycles through the ISM, that the key physics of the ISM are revealed through spectrally resolved observations, and that the observations must cover a range of environments that spans the Milky Way, the Magellantic Clouds, and

(i) atomic carbon fine-structure lines are the most powerful tool for the study of the dark molecular ISM, (ii) CO mid-J lines are the most important tracer of the warm, dense ISM, (iii) both sets of lines can only be observed with a large survey covering the entire Galactic disk, the Galactic Center and the Magellanic Clouds, and (iv) the observations will be complemented with (chemical) models and simulations of the ISM.

(i) the cycling of matter from the ISM to stars and back can only be understood through the combined analysis of observations and modelling of the ISM; (ii) the key observational tracers for this analysis are the fine-structure lines of atomic carbon and CO mid-J transitions; and (iii) the next decade and the next generation of observatories (e.g., ALMA, SKA, JWST, Athena, and Euclid) will allow us to address this key science

the following questions: How does the interstellar medium evolve from its initial state to the state in which stars form? What is the origin of the observed diversity of star forming regions? How does the intergalactic medium evolve and what are the conditions for star formation in dwarf galaxies?

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

a comprehensive and detailed understanding of the interstellar cycle of matter in galaxies requires observations and modelling of a wide range of molecular and atomic gas phases and a wide range of physical conditions.

a large scale survey of the Galactic molecular clouds, Magellanic Clouds, and nearby galaxies is needed to understand the cycling of matter in galaxies and the formation of structure in the interstellar gas.

the next decade is a unique opportunity for a comprehensive survey of Galactic molecular clouds and nearby galaxies to address the open questions regarding the cycling of matter from the interstellar medium to stars and back.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

a detailed understanding of the matter cycle in galaxies requires observations of the atomic and molecular gas over a wide range of physical conditions and environments, and the combination of the observational results with modelling.
we need to understand the cycling of matter in galaxies from the assembly and fragmentation of clouds to the feedback of stars and AGN.

the matter cycle from interstellar medium to stars and back is a complex and highly non-linear process, which can only be fully understood with observations of a large variety of tracers in combination with simulations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a comprehensive understanding of the cycling of matter in the interstellar media of galaxies is possible, if we can measure the full range of physical conditions and environments.

the next decade will provide us with an unprecedented wealth of observational data, which, if properly interpreted in the context of modelling and simulations, will lead to a better understanding of the matter cycle and thus the star formation history of our Universe.
the proposed observations will be crucial to address fundamental questions about the interstellar medium and its role in star formation.
